title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback for students’ open-ended mathematics responses. The authors focus on two related questions: how well different models can predict teacher-assigned scores for student answers, and how useful the feedback generated by those models is when judged by human evaluators. The study is motivated by the growing use of online learning platforms in math education and the challenge of providing timely, individualized feedback on open-ended work.

The authors compare three approaches: SBERT-Canberra, a prior similarity-based automated assessment method; GOAT, a fine-tuned Mistral 7B model trained on student responses and teacher-written scores/feedback; and GPT-4 Turbo, used in a zero-shot prompting setup with a rubric based on Illustrative Mathematics. The dataset came from an online learning platform and included 50 open-response middle-school math problems, each with 100 student answers, teacher scores, and teacher feedback messages. The models were trained/evaluated on an 80/20 split, yielding 4,000 training entries and 1,000 test entries. In addition to quantitative scoring metrics (AUC, RMSE, Cohen’s kappa), two educators qualitatively evaluated feedback on 100 sampled test responses for accuracy, relevance, motivation, and overall preference.

The context is middle-school mathematics in an online learning platform using Illustrative Mathematics-style open-ended tasks and a 0–4 scoring rubric. The study also incorporates teacher involvement in two ways: historical teacher-provided scores/feedback served as training data, and two educators with prior teaching experience rated generated feedback. The paper does not test student learning gains directly; instead, it evaluates the performance of AI systems against teacher scoring and teacher judgments of feedback quality.

The main findings are that the fine-tuned GOAT model performed best on the auto-scoring task, outperforming SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on AUC, RMSE, and kappa. However, GPT-4 was clearly preferred for feedback generation, receiving the highest ratings for accuracy, relevance, and overall preference from human evaluators. The authors conclude that fine-tuned open-source LLMs show promise for automated math assessment, especially for scoring, but that feedback quality remains limited by the quality of teacher-authored training data. They argue that future work should refine datasets and improve feedback quality before broad deployment.

identified_tools.name: Mistral
identified_tools.description: An open-source large language model family by Mistral AI. In this paper, Mistral 7B is fine-tuned into a bespoke system for math open-response scoring and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned as the GOAT model on teacher-scored middle-school math open responses to generate numeric scores and textual feedback for students' open-ended math answers.

findings.finding_summary: The fine-tuned GOAT model based on Mistral outperformed both SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on the auto-scoring task for open-ended math responses. On the 1,000-entry test set, GOAT achieved AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Kappa=0.422, versus SBERT (AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, Kappa=0.362) and GPT-4 (AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, Kappa=0.266).
findings.measure: Teacher-score prediction on open-ended math responses using AUC, RMSE, and multi-class Cohen's Kappa

findings.finding_summary: For feedback generation, the fine-tuned GOAT model was judged better than SBERT-Canberra but worse than GPT-4 by two human evaluators reviewing 100 sampled test entries. GOAT reached 68% consensus accuracy, 88% consensus relevance, 48% motivating feedback, 5% demotivating feedback, and was selected as the preferred model 12% of the time on average.
findings.measure: Human evaluation of generated feedback on accuracy, relevance, motivation, demotivation, and preference

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family of large language models. In this paper, GPT-4 Turbo is used zero-shot with a rubric prompt to score and provide feedback on students' math open responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a zero-shot setup with the problem, student answer, and scoring rubric to generate both a score and concise feedback for middle-school open-ended math responses.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4 underperformed the fine-tuned GOAT model and SBERT-Canberra on the scoring task, though it had lower RMSE than SBERT. On the 1,000-entry test set, GPT-4 achieved AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, and Kappa=0.266.
findings.measure: Teacher-score prediction on open-ended math responses using AUC, RMSE, and multi-class Cohen's Kappa

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4 was the strongest model for feedback generation according to two human evaluators reviewing 100 sampled test entries. It achieved 86% consensus accuracy, 91% consensus relevance, 52% motivating feedback, 1% demotivating feedback, and was preferred 77.5% of the time on average over GOAT and SBERT.
findings.measure: Human evaluation of generated feedback on accuracy, relevance, motivation, demotivation, and preference

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic automated scoring and feedback approach for student open responses. In this paper, this corresponds to the SBERT-Canberra similarity-based method used to recommend scores and feedback from historical responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the prior state-of-the-art baseline for scoring and feedback on students' open-ended math responses by retrieving similar historical responses and associated teacher scores/feedback.

findings.finding_summary: The SBERT-Canberra baseline performed below GOAT on all scoring metrics and below GPT-4 on RMSE, but remained competitive as the second-highest model on AUC and Kappa. On the 1,000-entry test set, it achieved AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, and Kappa=0.362.
findings.measure: Teacher-score prediction on open-ended math responses using AUC, RMSE, and multi-class Cohen's Kappa

findings.finding_summary: SBERT-Canberra was the weakest of the three models in human evaluation of feedback quality on 100 sampled test entries. It achieved 52% consensus accuracy, 76% consensus relevance, 46% motivating feedback, 11% demotivating feedback, and was preferred 12% of the time on average.
findings.measure: Human evaluation of generated feedback on accuracy, relevance, motivation, demotivation, and preference

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical comparative study with held-out test evaluation and human ratings, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental study of student learning outcomes. The evidence is based on model performance against teacher scores and teacher judgments of feedback quality.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear differences in automated scoring and feedback quality across tools, but does not report standardized learning effect sizes or direct student outcome impacts. Impact on learning is therefore promising but unclear.
